title: How to Read the Bible Without Making It Say What You Want
excerpt: Two sincere readers open the same page and find opposite gods. The problem is not that the Bible is unclear. It is that no one reads from nowhere.
body:
Two readers open the same page of Paul's letter to the Romans. One closes it certain that God has blessed the social order exactly as it stands, that submission to authority is the whole of Christian duty. The other closes it certain that God is the great leveler who would pull that order down and seat the poor at the head of the table. Both are sincere. Both are literate. Both have read the same words in the same order, and both have walked out of the room carrying a different god. This happens every Sunday, in every tradition, in every century the church has had a book. It is the oldest problem we have.

The problem is not that the Bible is unclear. The problem is that we are not neutral, and we have spent five hundred years pretending we are.

That pretense has a history, and like most of the things that own us, it began as something good. When the Reformers said sola scriptura and put the Bible into the hands of the plowboy, they were not handing out a license for everyone to invent a private faith. They were breaking a monopoly. Scripture, they insisted, was clear enough in the things that matter for salvation that an ordinary believer could read it and live. They called this perspicuity, and they were right about it. But the printing press and the centuries that followed did something the Reformers did not intend. They produced a new character who has haunted the Western mind ever since. The reader who believes he stands nowhere. The mind that imagines it can approach the text the way Descartes imagined he could approach everything, scrubbed clean of every inheritance, a neutral observer reporting only what is there.

There is no such reader. There never was.

Begin with the strongest case for the side I am about to disagree with, because it deserves it. The plain-reading instinct is not stupidity. It is reverence wearing work clothes. The person who says just tell me what the text says and I will do it is protecting something precious, the conviction that God has spoken and that his word stands over us rather than under us. Mark Noll has documented how this instinct, what he calls a Reformed, commonsense biblicism, built American evangelical religion and gave it its spine (Noll 1994). When a believer resists the scholar who seems to dissolve every command into context, that believer is guarding the possibility that the Bible can still tell him to do something he does not want to do. That is not a small thing to guard. A book you can interpret into anything is a book that can no longer command you.

Grant all of it. Then notice what the plain reading cannot account for.

The same Americans who held the plainest, highest view of the Bible in the world read it, in 1845, straight into the defense of human slavery. They were not lying. They were not, most of them, cynics looking for a proof-text to cover an evil they already loved. They opened the book, found Paul returning Onesimus to his master, found the household codes, found no explicit abolition, and concluded in good conscience that the plain sense of Scripture permitted what their economy required. The abolitionists, working from the same book, lost the exegetical argument in the eyes of most and won the moral one in the eyes of history. Noll calls this the theological crisis of the Civil War, and it is the permanent refutation of the myth of the innocent reader (Noll 2006). The plainest readers in the country read the plain text and baptized an atrocity. The text did not fail them. Their certainty that they brought nothing to it failed them.

There is no reading without a reader, and the reader is never empty.

Now the other side, and it gets its full weight too. The progressive instinct says exactly what I have just said. There is no neutral reading. Every interpretation is shaped by the community, the century, the wound, the interest of the one doing the interpreting. The patriarch reads patriarchy, the empire reads empire, the comfortable read comfort. Hans-Georg Gadamer gave this its most serious philosophical form. We never come to a text as blank minds, he argued. We come carrying what he called prejudices, prejudgments, the whole inheritance of language and history that makes understanding possible in the first place. Understanding is not the erasure of our horizon but the fusion of our horizon with the horizon of the text (Gadamer 1989). The reader who claims to have no lens is simply a reader who has not noticed his glasses.

This is true. It is so true that the church has known it for sixteen centuries and the modern skeptic is late to it. Augustine said it in the fourth century, that anyone who thinks he has understood the Scriptures but whose interpretation does not build up the love of God and neighbor has not yet understood them at all (Augustine 1997). He assumed what Gadamer rediscovered, that we read from somewhere, toward something, with our loves already engaged.

But watch what happens when this true observation is asked to do more work than it can bear. If every reading is only the projection of the reader's interest, then the slaveholder and the abolitionist are simply two communities with two preferences and no court above them to which either can appeal. The text becomes a mirror. You look in, and you find your own face, and you call it God. Kevin Vanhoozer named the danger precisely in the title of his great book, asking whether there is any meaning in the text at all, or only the meanings we bring (Vanhoozer 1998). If the answer is only what we bring, then Scripture cannot correct us, because there is nothing in it that is not already us. The prophet cannot indict the king, because the prophet is only the king's rival reading. The progressive who weaponizes interpretation against the fundamentalist has, without noticing, dismantled the one tool that could ever have been used against injustice. A book that can mean anything means nothing, and a book that means nothing has never once set a captive free.

So both certainties collapse. The plain reading collapses because there is no innocent reader. The everything-is-interpretation reading collapses because it leaves the reader trapped in the mirror with no word from outside. Each is half of a truth pretending to be the whole.

The honest fact that no one reads from nowhere does not drive us toward relativism. Followed all the way down, it drives us back to exactly the things the modern reader was trying to escape, the community, the tradition, and the rule of faith. If I cannot trust my own neutrality, then I cannot be my own magisterium. The recognition that I read through a lens is not permission to grind whatever lens I please. It is the reason I need other readers, dead ones and living ones, to grind it with me and to tell me when I have made the text into a flattering portrait of myself.

This is the move the buffered modern self resists most. Charles Taylor describes the self that emerged from the Enlightenment as one sealed off from outside influence, the sovereign individual who is his own authority and answers to no community he did not choose (Taylor 2007). That self reads the Bible alone, by definition, even when sitting in a crowded sanctuary, because it has already decided that no interpreter outside its own head has any claim on it. James K.A. Smith has spent his career pressing the point that we are not first thinkers but lovers, that our desires are trained by what we do long before our minds engage what we read, and so we arrive at the text already aimed (Smith 2009). The reader formed all week by the liturgies of self, the feed, the market, the nation, does not become neutral the moment he opens to the Gospel of Luke. The question was never whether you read through a lens. It is whose lens, ground by whom, and aimed at what.

There is a scene in the Old Testament that holds the whole of this, and the church has too often walked past it. In the eighth chapter of Nehemiah, the exiles have come home to a broken city, and they gather in the square, and they ask Ezra the scribe to bring the book. He reads it aloud from morning until midday, and the people stand the whole time. But the reading is not left to fall on the crowd unaided. The Levites moved among the people and helped them understand, and the phrase is worth its weight. They read from the book, from the law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading (Nehemiah 8:8 ESV).

They gave the sense. The word of God was read plainly, and it still required to be opened. There is no opposition here between the authority of the text and the labor of interpretation. The same scene holds both. The book stands over the people. The people cannot grasp the book without help. And the help is not a single expert descending with the answers. It is the whole company of teachers moving through the assembly, a community formed around the text, doing together what no one of them could do alone.

Then comes the part that exposes every reader's heart. When the people understand, they weep. The word has done its work, it has shown them the distance between the life they have lived and the life the law describes, and they break. And Nehemiah and Ezra tell them to stop weeping, to go and eat the fat and drink the sweet wine and send portions to those who have nothing, because the joy of the Lord is their strength. The right reading of the text moves through grief into grace, and out the far side into generosity toward the poor. A reading that ends in despair has stopped too soon. A reading that never passed through the grief was never serious. And a reading that does not finally send bread to the one who has none has not understood the book at all.

This is not a technique. It is the gospel applied to the act of reading, and the cross is what makes it possible.

The reason I cannot be trusted alone with the text is the same reason I cannot be trusted alone with anything, the simple fact named on the first pages of the book, that the human heart curves inward and bends every good gift back toward itself. I do not read the Bible from a neutral place because there is no neutral place in me. There is a will that wants to be justified, and it will go into the holiest book ever written and come out holding a verse that proves it was right all along. Left to myself, I will always find the God I came looking for. That is not a flaw in my method. It is the condition the cross exists to address.

To read Scripture as a Christian is to submit to a text that intends to put me to death before it raises me. It means going to the page expecting to be contradicted, not confirmed. It means treating the verse that wounds me as more likely to be God's word to me than the verse that flatters me, because the God of this book has never once been the projection of human desire and has always been its interruption. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, teaching his underground seminarians to read, told them to come to the Scriptures as a servant comes to his master, not as a master comes to a servant (Bonhoeffer 1954). He was describing the death that has to happen on the way into the text. The reader who will not die over the page will only ever be reading himself.

I know this reader. I have been this reader. I have stood with a passage on a Saturday night that meant to break something in me and in my people, and I have felt my mind go to work softening it, finding the angle that would let me preach it without being indicted by it, the reading that would cost the congregation something and cost me nothing. That is not interpretation. It is the oldest evasion there is, the one the serpent taught in the garden when he asked the first hermeneutical question ever recorded, did God really say. Every dishonest reading of Scripture since has been a footnote to that sentence. We do not usually deny the word. We adjust it, until it agrees with us, and we call the adjustment study.

So the practices that follow are not tips. They are the shape of a death and a resurrection, worked out in the ordinary discipline of opening the book.

Read it with the dead and the living, never alone. The whole point of the rule of faith, the creeds, the long tradition of the church, is that they are the lens-grinders God has given you so that you do not have to trust your own eyes by themselves. When your reading of a passage is one that no Christian in two thousand years has ever held, the odds are not that you have finally seen clearly. The odds are that you have found your own face in the mirror. Read with your enemies too. Read the brother across the political aisle who finds in the text what you cannot find, because he is reading past your blind spot the way you are reading past his.

Read the parts that condemn you first. Go looking for the sentence you do not want, and when you find it, stay there. The verse that offends your politics, your appetite, your certainty, is the verse most likely to be doing the work the gospel sent it to do, because grace comes through the wound and not around it. A reading that never makes you weep in the square has not yet read you.

And then do the last thing Nehemiah commanded. Send a portion to the one who has none. The test of whether you have read the book rightly is never the elegance of your interpretation. It is whether the reading drove you out of the mirror and into your neighbor's need. The Scripture was never given so that you could be right about it. It was given so that you could be remade by it, and the proof of the remaking is bread in another person's hand.

The Bible is not a mirror, though we keep using it as one. It is a window, and on the far side of it stands a God who has never yet been the thing we wanted him to be, and has always been the thing we needed. You will spend your whole life learning the difference. The learning is the Christian life. And the day you are certain you have finally read it without bending it to yourself is the day you should be most afraid, because that is the day the mirror has won and you have not even noticed the glass.

Read like a person who expects to be told something true and unwelcome. It is the only way anyone has ever heard from God.

### Works Cited

Augustine. 1997. On Christian Teaching. Translated by R. P. H. Green. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

Bonhoeffer, Dietrich. 1954. Life Together. Translated by John W. Doberstein. New York: Harper and Row.

Gadamer, Hans-Georg. 1989. Truth and Method. 2nd rev. ed. New York: Crossroad.

Noll, Mark A. 1994. The Scandal of the Evangelical Mind. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Noll, Mark A. 2006. The Civil War as a Theological Crisis. Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press.

Smith, James K. A. 2009. Desiring the Kingdom. Grand Rapids: Baker Academic.

Taylor, Charles. 2007. A Secular Age. Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press.

Vanhoozer, Kevin J. 1998. Is There a Meaning in This Text? Grand Rapids: Zondervan.

title: What the Gospel Actually Is
excerpt: The gospel is not advice about how to be good or how to feel loved. It is news about something God has done. And news is more demanding than advice.
body:
A man stops you on the street and tells you the war is over. He does not tell you to end the war. He does not give you seven steps for ending wars, or assure you that deep down the war was already over inside your heart. He tells you a thing that happened. The guns are silent. The enemy has surrendered. Go home.

That is what the word gospel means, and we have nearly lost it. Euangelion, the Greek word the New Testament uses, was not a religious word when the church took it. It was a word from the herald and the battlefield, the announcement of a victory or the birth of an emperor. An inscription carved in the marketplace of Priene around the year 9 before Christ called the birthday of Caesar Augustus good news, euangelion, for the whole world, the arrival of a savior who would end war and order the earth (Wright 2015). The first Christians knew exactly what they were doing when they took that word. They walked into the empire's own vocabulary and said the real good news, the actual turning point of history, is not the birth of the emperor. It is the death and resurrection of a crucified Galilean. The gospel was a counter-announcement before it was anything else. It was news, and it was treason.

We have turned it back into advice.

Take the strongest version of the first way we do that, because it is the sincere one. The gospel, many good people will tell you, is the call to follow the example of Jesus, to love your neighbor, to live the Sermon on the Mount, to be a decent and compassionate human being. This instinct is guarding something real. It will not let faith collapse into a private feeling that changes nothing about how a person treats the poor or the enemy. It remembers that Jesus said depart from me to people who called him Lord and did nothing. A gospel that produces no life is a corpse, and the moralist is right to refuse it.

But follow the instinct to its end. If the gospel is fundamentally advice about how to live, then it is not news, and it is not good. It is a ladder, and you already know how the ladder ends, because you have been climbing some version of it your whole life and you are tired, and you are not at the top, and the rung you are standing on will not hold your weight much longer. Advice assumes the war can still be won by the listener. The whole problem is that it cannot.

Now the other way, the gentler one. The gospel, a great many will tell you, is simply that God loves you exactly as you are, full stop, no conditions, no demands. This too guards something precious. It refuses to let grace become a transaction, refuses the cruelty of a God you must satisfy before he will have you. It remembers that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, that the love came first and uninvited. The sociologist Christian Smith, studying what American teenagers actually believe, found that this had become the real religion of the country, a creed he named moralistic therapeutic deism, in which God exists mainly to make people feel good about themselves and to be available when needed (Smith 2005). It is gentle. It is not nothing. It is half of something true.

But severed from the cross, that love becomes mere sentiment, a warmth that asks for nothing and therefore changes nothing and therefore cost nothing. Dietrich Bonhoeffer named it in 1937 and the name has never been bettered. Cheap grace is the grace we bestow on ourselves, the preaching of forgiveness without requiring repentance, grace without the cross, grace without Jesus Christ (Bonhoeffer 1937). A love that cost the lover nothing is not the love the New Testament is talking about. The love the New Testament is talking about has a body and the body has wounds.

Both ways make the gospel something about you, your effort or your worth. Paul refused both. When he set down what he meant by the gospel, in the fifteenth chapter of his first letter to Corinth, he did not give an ethic and he did not give a reassurance. He gave a report. I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received, that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day, and that he appeared, to Peter, to the twelve, to more than five hundred at once, most of whom are still alive (1 Corinthians 15:3-6 ESV). It is a list of events with a list of witnesses, datable, public, the kind of claim that can be checked and therefore the kind of claim that can be false. J. Gresham Machen, watching the faith dissolve into ethical idealism in 1923, put it as plainly as it can be put. Christianity is founded not upon an idea but upon a piece of information. From the beginning the gospel was news (Machen 1923).

And the news has a center, and the center is the cross, and the cross is doing the work, not decorating the end of it. Christ died for our sins. The little word for is the engine. It means the death was in our place, that the war we could not win was won by someone else taking the loss that was ours to take. You cannot hear this as good news until the bad news has landed, until you have understood that you are not the neutral civilian in this story but the losing side, that the thing the cross addresses is not your low self-esteem but your guilt. The order matters more than almost anything in the Christian life. Grace offered before the law has done its work is cheap, and grace withheld after the law has done its work is cruelty. Tim Keller spent his ministry on one sentence about this. The gospel is neither religion nor irreligion, neither the moralist's ladder nor the libertine's shrug, but a third thing the world keeps failing to imagine, that we are more sinful than we ever dared believe and more loved than we ever dared hope, at the same time, in the same act, on the same cross.

Here is the reversal the comfortable reader never sees coming. This is more demanding than any moral program, not less. The ladder asks only for improvement, a better version of the self you already are. The gospel asks for that self's death. It does not want your behavior tidied. It wants the whole man handed over, the will, the record, the future, exchanged for a life you did not earn and cannot manage and will spend the rest of your days learning to receive. Grace is not the absence of demand. It is the most total demand there is, because it claims everything, and it gives everything, and there is nothing left over that is still yours to control. Cheap grace is easy because it leaves you on the throne. The real thing costs you the throne.

I have preached the advice and called it the gospel. I have stood up on a Sunday and sent people home to try harder, to be kinder, to do better this week, and called that the good news of Jesus Christ, and it was the moralist's sermon wearing a worship band's clothes. I have done it because advice is safe and news is dangerous. Advice keeps me useful, the helpful expert with the steps. News makes me a beggar telling other beggars where the bread is, with nothing to offer but the announcement and no way to improve on it. The pull toward advice is the pull away from the cross, and I feel it every week.

The herald does not ask you to win the war. He tells you it has already been won, somewhere outside the city, on a hill, by someone else, and the telling is either the best thing you have ever heard or an offense, depending entirely on whether you still wanted to fight it yourself. Good news to the soldier who is exhausted and out of ammunition and ready to lay it down. Treason to the one who was sure he was winning. The gospel has always been both, and which one it is to you tells you exactly where you are standing.

### Works Cited

Bonhoeffer, Dietrich. 1937. The Cost of Discipleship. Translated by R. H. Fuller. New York: Macmillan.

Keller, Timothy. 2008. The Reason for God. New York: Dutton.

Machen, J. Gresham. 1923. Christianity and Liberalism. New York: Macmillan.

Smith, Christian, with Melinda Lundquist Denton. 2005. Soul Searching: The Religious and Spiritual Lives of American Teenagers. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

Wright, N. T. 2015. Simply Good News. New York: HarperOne.

title: The Trinity Is Not Optional
excerpt: We treat the Trinity as the church's embarrassing arithmetic. It is the most practical claim Christianity makes, and the ground everyone is standing on.
body:
A child asks how God can be three and also one, and the adults at the table change the subject. We have made the Trinity the church's embarrassing arithmetic, the doctrine we recite in the creed on Sunday and never once use on Monday, the freight we haul because the councils told us to. We can explain why the cross matters and why grace matters and why prayer matters. Ask most believers why it matters that God is triune and you will get a long pause and a diagram involving water or an egg.

This is exactly backward. The doctrine no one uses is the ground everyone is standing on.

Give the skeptic the full force of the objection first, because it is a serious one. The word Trinity is not in the Bible. The fully developed doctrine was hammered out over three centuries and finalized at councils that emperors convened, beginning with Nicaea in the year 325, summoned by Constantine, who cared at least as much about imperial unity as about theology. The fights were political and often ugly. Athanasius, the doctrine's great defender, was driven into exile five times. And on its face the claim looks like incoherence, one equals three, or like later Greek philosophy bolted onto the plain monotheism of a Jewish prophet who only ever told people to worship the God of Israel. Stated that way, the suspicion is understandable. A reasonable person could conclude the church invented a riddle and then demanded everyone affirm it.

Grant the mess. The councils were human and the politics were real. But the doctrine was not an imposition laid on top of the New Testament. It was a synthesis forced out from underneath it, the church's refusal to drop any of the things the text would not let it drop.

The first Christians were Jews. They said the Shema every day, hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one, and they meant it with their lives, and they died rather than grant that Caesar was a god. And these same fierce monotheists prayed to Jesus, sang to him as Lord, baptized in the threefold name, and described the Spirit as God present and personal among them. They did not arrive at the Trinity by speculation. They were driven to it by the refusal to let go of four things all at once. The Father is God. Jesus is worshipped as God. The Spirit is God. There is one God. Arius, in the fourth century, offered a clean way out. Make the Son a high and glorious creature, the first and best thing God made, but a creature, not God himself. It solved the math. The church looked at the solution and saw that it dissolved the gospel, because a creature cannot save, and a Savior you worship who is less than God is an idol however exalted. At Nicaea the church answered Arius with a single word that is not elegant and was never meant to be, homoousios, of the same being as the Father. Athanasius spent his whole hunted life on that one word because he saw what it was protecting (Athanasius 2011).

What it was protecting is most visible not in a creed but in a prayer. On the night before he died, in the seventeenth chapter of John, Jesus prays aloud, and the prayer opens a window into the inside of God. He speaks to the Father of a glory the two of them shared before the world existed. He speaks of being loved by the Father before the foundation of the world. And he prays that his people would be brought inside that very love, that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you (John 17:21-24 ESV). The doctrine of the Trinity is, in the end, only the church learning to say what that prayer takes for granted. Before there was a universe to love, there was love. The Father loved the Son. The love did not begin when creatures arrived to receive it.

This is the thing the doctrine secures, and everything turns on it. Love is not something God started doing when he made a world. Love is what God is, eternally, in himself, three persons giving and receiving without beginning and without end. The Greek fathers had a word for the way the persons make room for one another in this endless mutual life, perichoresis, a kind of eternal indwelling. Augustine spent fifteen books circling it, finally finding its trace in the structure of love itself, which always requires a lover, a beloved, and the love that passes between them (Augustine 1991). C. S. Lewis, trying to get ordinary readers to feel it, said that God is not a static thing but a dynamic, pulsating activity, a life, almost a kind of dance (Lewis 1952).

Now the reversal, the thing the bored Sunday believer never expects. This is the most practical claim Christianity makes. Imagine the alternative were true, that God is a single solitary power, a lonely monad on the throne of the universe. Then God needed the world in order to have anything to love, which means love is something God takes up, a later activity, and the most basic thing about ultimate reality is not love but sheer undifferentiated power and will. A universe with a unitarian god at the top is a universe in which force is more fundamental than love, and the self that images that god will believe, all the way down, that power is what finally matters and relationship is what you do once power is secured. But if God is triune, then the deepest fact about all that exists is not force and not the lonely will. It is self-giving love between persons, older than time. Catherine LaCugna argued that this is the entire point, that the doctrine is not abstract at all but tells us reality itself is personal and relational at its root (LaCugna 1991).

That detonates the central myth of the modern self. Charles Taylor describes the self the Enlightenment built as buffered and sovereign, the individual who imagines he is most free when he owes nothing to anyone and answers to no one he did not choose (Taylor 2007). The Trinity says the opposite is the truth of things. You were made in the image of a God who is community, whose very being is gift, and so you become most yourself not by self-possession but by self-donation, not by guarding your life but by giving it away. The lonely autonomous self is not the height of freedom. It is a small imitation of the lonely god who does not exist.

And the cross is the Trinity made visible in time. On Golgotha the Son gives himself, the Father gives the Son, the Spirit holds them across the dark. Strip out the Trinity and the cross becomes a horror, one being punishing another being to satisfy his anger, which is the caricature the critics rightly despise. Hold the Trinity and the cross is God giving himself, the eternal self-gift of Father, Son, and Spirit reaching into history and going all the way down into death and out the other side. Karl Barth insisted that God's very being is this act, that God is the one who loves in freedom, and that what happened on the cross was not foreign to God but the truest revelation of who God has always been (Barth 1957).

I will confess that I have treated this doctrine as a museum piece, something to defend against heretics rather than something to live inside. I have preached a God of love on Sunday and then spent the week ordering my life as though the basic structure of reality were competition and self-protection, getting mine, securing my position, keeping score. That is functional unitarianism. It is the practical worship of a single solitary power, whatever I say in the creed. The way a man guards his own life gives away the god he actually believes in, and mine has too often been the lonely one.

The child's question was the right question, and changing the subject was the failure. How can God be three and one. The answer is that God is love, and love has never been able to exist alone, because love requires one who loves and one who is loved and the love itself that binds them, and so the God who is love has never once been solitary, and was never going to make us to be solitary either. He made us to be brought inside the oldest love there is. The doctrine you thought was useless is the reason you exist and the home you are being called into. That is not arithmetic. That is the whole thing.

### Works Cited

Athanasius. 2011. On the Incarnation. Translated by John Behr. Yonkers, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press.

Augustine. 1991. The Trinity. Translated by Edmund Hill. Brooklyn: New City Press.

Barth, Karl. 1957. Church Dogmatics II.1. Edinburgh: T and T Clark.

LaCugna, Catherine Mowry. 1991. God for Us: The Trinity and Christian Life. San Francisco: HarperSanFrancisco.

Lewis, C. S. 1952. Mere Christianity. London: Geoffrey Bles.

Taylor, Charles. 2007. A Secular Age. Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press.
